title: EC2 - V2
body:
🔥 SECTION 1: INSTANCE TYPES (In-Depth)

📖 Understanding EC2 Instance Naming

Format: m5.xlarge

  • m = Family (General Purpose)
  • 5 = Generation (newer = better price/performance)
  • xlarge = Size (nano → micro → small → medium → large → xlarge → 2xlarge → ... → 24xlarge)

Additional letters:

  • a = AMD processor (cheaper, e.g., m5a)
  • g = Graviton (ARM, AWS's own chip — best price/performance)
  • n = Network-optimized (e.g., c5n — more bandwidth)
  • d = NVMe instance storage included
  • i = Intel processor (newer Intel gen)
  • e = Extra memory/storage

🔑 Instance Family Deep Dive

1️⃣ T-Family (Burstable) — T3, T3a, T4g

How it works: Runs at a baseline CPU % (e.g., 20%). When you need more CPU, it uses CPU credits earned while idle.

Modes:

  • T3 Standard: Runs out of credits → throttled to baseline
  • T3 Unlimited: Can burst forever → pay extra when credits run out

✅ Use Cases:

  • Development/test environments
  • Small websites, blogs, WordPress
  • Microservices with inconsistent traffic
  • Low-traffic APIs
  • Code repositories

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Low traffic, bursty, cost-sensitive, dev/test" → T-family

2️⃣ M-Family (General Purpose) — M5, M6i, M6g, M7i

Balanced CPU, memory, and network. The default choice when requirements aren't extreme.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Web application servers
  • Small-to-medium databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL)
  • Enterprise business apps (SAP, SharePoint)
  • Backend API servers
  • Caching fleets

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Balanced workload, general web/app server" → M-family

3️⃣ C-Family (Compute Optimized) — C5, C6i, C6g, C7g

Highest CPU-to-memory ratio. Designed for CPU-heavy tasks.

✅ Use Cases:

  • HPC (High-Performance Computing) — simulations, modeling
  • Batch processing — video encoding, data transformation
  • Gaming servers — dedicated multiplayer hosting
  • Scientific computing — genomics, weather modeling
  • Ad serving engines
  • ML inference (CPU-based, not GPU)

🎯 Exam Trigger: "CPU-intensive, HPC, batch, gaming, scientific computing" → C-family

4️⃣ R-Family (Memory Optimized) — R5, R6i, R6g, R7iz

High RAM relative to CPU. For in-memory workloads.

✅ Use Cases:

  • In-memory databases (Redis, Memcached, ElastiCache)
  • High-performance relational DBs (MySQL, PostgreSQL with large buffer pool)
  • Real-time big data analytics (Apache Spark, Presto)
  • Enterprise apps with large caching needs
  • Elasticsearch clusters

🎯 Exam Trigger: "In-memory DB, Redis, large dataset in memory" → R-family

5️⃣ X-Family (Extreme Memory) — X1, X1e, X2idn, X2iedn

Massive RAM (up to 24 TB!). Extreme memory-bound workloads.

✅ Use Cases:

  • SAP HANA (the #1 exam association)
  • In-memory databases at huge scale
  • Electronic Design Automation (EDA)
  • Financial services big data

🎯 Exam Trigger: "SAP HANA, huge in-memory workloads" → X-family

6️⃣ I-Family (Storage — NVMe SSD) — I3, I3en, I4i, Im4gn

Local NVMe SSDs, extremely high IOPS & low latency.

✅ Use Cases:

  • NoSQL databases (Cassandra, MongoDB, ScyllaDB)
  • Transactional DBs needing low-latency storage
  • Search engines (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch)
  • Data warehousing
  • Real-time analytics

🎯 Exam Trigger: "High IOPS, NoSQL, low-latency local storage" → I-family

7️⃣ D-Family (Storage — HDD) — D2, D3, D3en

Dense HDD storage, massive capacity (up to 336 TB per instance).

✅ Use Cases:

  • Hadoop / HDFS clusters
  • MapReduce data processing
  • Distributed file systems
  • Data warehousing (less latency-sensitive)
  • Log processing

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Data warehouse, Hadoop, MapReduce, massive HDD" → D-family

8️⃣ P-Family (GPU — ML Training) — P3, P4, P4d, P5

Powerful GPUs (NVIDIA V100, A100, H100) for training massive ML models.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Deep learning training (LLMs, transformers, GPT-style)
  • Large-scale GPU compute
  • High-performance computing with GPU acceleration
  • Molecular simulations

🎯 Exam Trigger: "ML training, deep learning, GPU compute" → P-family

9️⃣ G-Family (GPU — Graphics) — G4, G5, G6

GPU-optimized for graphics workloads (less expensive than P).

✅ Use Cases:

  • Video transcoding / rendering
  • 3D visualization, CAD/CAE
  • Game streaming (cloud gaming)
  • ML inference (not training)
  • Remote workstations with GPU

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Graphics, video rendering, 3D, cloud gaming" → G-family

🔟 Inf-Family (ML Inference) — Inf1, Inf2

AWS's own Inferentia chips, optimized for ML inference at low cost.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Real-time ML prediction (fraud detection, recommendations)
  • NLP inference at scale
  • Image/video recognition pipelines

🎯 Exam Trigger: "ML inference, low-cost prediction" → Inf-family

1️⃣1️⃣ Trn-Family (ML Training) — Trn1

AWS's own Trainium chips, designed to reduce cost of ML training vs. GPU.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Training deep learning models at lower cost than P-family

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Cost-effective ML training" → Trn-family

1️⃣2️⃣ Graviton (ARM) — Suffix "g" (M6g, C7g, R7g)

AWS's custom ARM-based processors. Up to 40% better price/performance than x86.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Any workload that can recompile for ARM (Linux, Java, Python, Node.js, .NET Core)
  • Cost-sensitive production fleets
  • Containerized microservices

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Best price/performance, cost optimization" → Graviton (g-suffix)

🔥 SECTION 2: PRICING MODELS (In-Depth)

💰 Full Pricing Breakdown

1️⃣ On-Demand

How it works: Pay per second (Linux) or per hour (Windows/commercial). No commitment.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Short-term apps (< 1 year)
  • Unpredictable workloads
  • Dev/test environments
  • First-time app deployment (testing demand)
  • Disaster recovery (temporary spike)

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Short-term, unpredictable, no commitment"

2️⃣ Reserved Instance (RI) — Standard

How it works: Commit to specific instance type for 1 or 3 years. Up to 72% discount.

Payment options:

  • All Upfront → max discount
  • Partial Upfront → mid discount
  • No Upfront → least discount

✅ Use Cases:

  • Production DBs running 24/7 (RDS, MySQL, PostgreSQL)
  • Application servers with steady traffic
  • Directory services (AD, DNS)
  • Any always-on infra for 1+ year

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Steady-state, always running, known workload"

3️⃣ Reserved Instance — Convertible

Like Standard RI, but can change instance family, OS, tenancy during the term. ~54% discount.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Long-term commitment when architecture might change
  • Migrating from M-family to C-family later
  • Evolving application needs

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Need to change instance family later"

4️⃣ Compute Savings Plan

How it works: Commit to $X per hour of compute spend for 1 or 3 years. Up to 66% discount.

Flexibility:

  • ✅ Any EC2 family
  • ✅ Any region
  • ✅ Any OS
  • ✅ Works for Fargate & Lambda too!

✅ Use Cases:

  • Multi-workload environments (EC2 + Lambda + Fargate)
  • Organizations wanting flexibility over lock-in
  • Global deployments across regions

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Flexibility across services and regions"

5️⃣ EC2 Instance Savings Plan

How it works: Commit to specific instance family in specific region. Up to 72% discount (same as RI).

Flexibility within commitment:

  • ✅ Any size in family
  • ✅ Any AZ in region
  • ✅ Any OS
  • ✅ Any tenancy

✅ Use Cases:

  • Mid-flexibility workloads (know family, not size)
  • Customers needing maximum discount with some flexibility

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Specific family in region, flexible on size"

6️⃣ Spot Instances

How it works: Use unused AWS capacity at up to 90% discount. AWS can reclaim with 2-minute warning.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Batch processing (ETL, data pipelines)
  • CI/CD build fleets
  • Big data analytics (Hadoop, Spark — resilient)
  • ML training (checkpoint frequently)
  • Image/video processing pipelines
  • Load testing

❌ NEVER for:

  • Production databases
  • Stateful web apps
  • Critical stateful workloads

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Fault-tolerant, stateless, flexible, interruptible"

Spot Fleet / EC2 Fleet

  • Mix Spot + On-Demand
  • Use multiple instance types for higher availability
  • 🎯 Exam Trigger: "Mix Spot and On-Demand to save cost"

7️⃣ Dedicated Host

How it works: Rent an entire physical server. You see sockets, cores, NUMA nodes. Most expensive.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Bring Your Own License (BYOL) — Windows Server, Oracle, SQL Server
  • Per-socket or per-core licensing compliance audits
  • Regulatory compliance (government, finance, healthcare)
  • Isolating workloads on specific hardware

🎯 Exam Trigger: "BYOL, per-socket license, compliance, regulatory"

8️⃣ Dedicated Instance

How it works: Instances on hardware dedicated to your account, but you don't see sockets/cores. Cheaper than Dedicated Host.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Hardware isolation for multi-tenant concerns
  • Compliance that requires isolation but not licensing visibility

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Hardware isolation only, no license concern"

Dedicated Host vs Dedicated Instance (🔥 Trap)

FeatureDedicated HostDedicated Instance
Physical server visibility✅❌
Socket/core visibility✅❌
BYOL support✅❌
CostHighestModerate

9️⃣ Capacity Reservations

How it works: Reserve capacity in a specific AZ — no discount, just guaranteed capacity.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Disaster recovery capacity guarantees
  • Big event launches (Black Friday, Super Bowl)
  • Ensuring capacity in specific AZs

Can combine with Savings Plan → get discount + guarantee.

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Guarantee capacity for specific event in AZ"

🎯 Complete Pricing Decision Flow

Need 24/7 same instance for 1-3 years?
   → Reserved Instance (Standard) — 72% off

Need flexibility across services (Lambda/Fargate)?
   → Compute Savings Plan — 66% off

Might change instance family in future?
   → Convertible RI — 54% off

Workload is fault-tolerant / stateless?
   → Spot — 90% off

Need per-socket license compliance?
   → Dedicated Host

Need hardware isolation only?
   → Dedicated Instance

Need guaranteed capacity (no discount)?
   → Capacity Reservation

Short-term unpredictable?
   → On-Demand

🔥 SECTION 3: STORAGE (EBS / Instance Store / EFS / FSx) — In-Depth

💾 EBS (Elastic Block Store) — Deep Dive

EBS Concept

  • Network-attached block storage (like a virtual hard drive)
  • AZ-locked (exists in ONE AZ only)
  • Persistent (survives instance stop/terminate if configured)
  • Can be detached and re-attached within same AZ

EBS Volume Types — In Detail

🔸 gp3 (General Purpose SSD — Current)

  • Max IOPS: 16,000
  • Max throughput: 1,000 MB/s
  • Size: 1 GiB – 16 TiB
  • IOPS decoupled from size → more cost-efficient than gp2
  • 20% cheaper than gp2 at the same size
  • Default choice for new workloads

✅ Use Cases:

  • Boot volumes
  • Medium-traffic web apps
  • Small-to-medium databases
  • Dev/test

🔸 gp2 (General Purpose SSD — Legacy)

  • Max IOPS: 16,000 (but scales at 3 IOPS per GB)
  • Must increase size to get more IOPS → wasteful
  • Replaced by gp3; avoid in new designs

🔸 io2 Block Express (Highest Performance)

  • Max IOPS: 256,000
  • Max throughput: 4,000 MB/s
  • Max size: 64 TiB
  • Sub-millisecond latency
  • 99.999% durability (5 nines — higher than standard EBS)

✅ Use Cases:

  • SAP HANA in production
  • Mission-critical relational DBs (Oracle, SQL Server, Postgres)
  • Real-time transaction processing

🔸 io1 / io2 (Provisioned IOPS SSD)

  • Max IOPS: 64,000
  • Multi-Attach supported (up to 16 Nitro instances, same AZ)
  • Pay for provisioned IOPS

✅ Use Cases:

  • Clustered DBs (Oracle RAC with cluster-aware file systems)
  • High-performance DBs
  • I/O-intensive production workloads

🔸 st1 (Throughput HDD)

  • Max IOPS: 500 (not IOPS-focused)
  • Max throughput: 500 MB/s
  • Optimized for sequential workloads

✅ Use Cases:

  • Big data (Hadoop, HDFS)
  • Log processing (streaming logs)
  • Data warehouses
  • ETL workloads

🔸 sc1 (Cold HDD)

  • Max IOPS: 250
  • Max throughput: 250 MB/s
  • Cheapest EBS option

✅ Use Cases:

  • Cold data archives
  • Rarely accessed backups
  • Long-term data storage needing block device interface

EBS Key Features

🔹 Snapshots

  • Point-in-time backups stored in S3 (AWS-managed, you don't see the bucket)
  • Incremental — only changed blocks are saved
  • Can be copied across regions → for DR
  • Can be shared with other accounts
  • Can create AMI from snapshot

✅ Use Cases:

  • Daily backups of production volumes
  • DR by copying snapshots to another region
  • Creating test environments from prod snapshots

🔹 Multi-Attach (io1/io2 only)

  • Up to 16 Nitro instances can attach to same volume in same AZ
  • Requires cluster-aware file system (e.g., GFS2, OCFS2)
  • Linux-only

✅ Use Cases:

  • Clustered DBs (Oracle RAC)
  • Active-active HA applications
  • Legacy clustered file systems

🔹 Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR)

  • Normally when you restore a volume from snapshot, blocks lazy-load on first access → slow initial performance.
  • FSR pre-warms the volume → full performance immediately.

✅ Use Cases:

  • Disaster recovery needing fast RTO
  • Cloning large volumes for immediate use
  • Golden image volumes for fast new instance launches

🔹 Encryption (via KMS)

  • Data at rest, in transit (between EC2 and EBS), snapshots, and volumes created from them — all encrypted.
  • To encrypt an unencrypted volume:
    1. Take snapshot
    2. Copy snapshot with encryption enabled
    3. Create new volume from encrypted snapshot

🔹 Delete on Termination

  • Root volume: DeleteOnTermination = true (default)
  • Additional volumes: DeleteOnTermination = false (default)
  • Adjustable per volume

💾 Instance Store (Ephemeral)

How it works: Physical SSDs attached directly to the host server. Data is lost when:

  • Instance stops
  • Instance hibernates
  • Instance fails (hardware)
  • Instance is terminated

BUT: Data survives reboot ✅

✅ Use Cases:

  • Buffer/cache for apps (Cassandra, Kafka)
  • Scratch data (temp processing)
  • Session state (with replication)
  • Data that can be regenerated

🎯 Exam Trap: "Data lost on stop" = Instance Store

💾 EFS (Elastic File System)

How it works: Fully managed NFSv4 file system for Linux. Shared across thousands of EC2s in multiple AZs.

Features:

  • Elastic — scales automatically
  • Multi-AZ — highly available
  • Pay per GB used (no provisioning)
  • Two performance modes: General Purpose / Max I/O
  • Two throughput modes: Bursting / Provisioned
  • Storage classes: Standard, Infrequent Access (IA), One Zone (cheaper)

✅ Use Cases:

  • WordPress fleet with shared media
  • Content Management Systems (Drupal, Joomla)
  • Shared home directories
  • Container persistent storage (ECS, EKS)
  • Big data analytics
  • Web serving with shared assets

🎯 Exam Trigger: "Shared Linux file system across multi-AZ" → EFS

💾 FSx Family

FSx for Windows File Server

  • SMB protocol, Windows-native
  • Active Directory integration
  • Windows ACLs, DFS namespaces

✅ Use Cases:

  • Windows user home directories
  • .NET application file shares
  • Windows-based enterprise apps
  • SharePoint on-prem migration

FSx for Lustre

  • HPC/ML file system — sub-millisecond latency, 100s of GB/s throughput
  • Integrates with S3 (data is accessible in Lustre + S3)

✅ Use Cases:

  • Machine learning training
  • Genomics analysis
  • Financial modeling
  • Media rendering
  • HPC simulations

FSx for NetApp ONTAP / OpenZFS

  • Enterprise-grade NAS with SnapMirror, SnapVault
  • Multi-protocol (NFS, SMB, iSCSI)

✅ Use Cases:

  • Migrating on-prem NetApp workloads
  • Enterprise apps needing NetApp features

⚖️ Storage Decision Guide

Single EC2 block storageEBS
Shared Linux file systemEFS
Shared Windows SMB/ADFSx for Windows
HPC/ML high-perf fileFSx for Lustre
Ultra-fast temp storageInstance Store

🔥 SECTION 4: AMI (Amazon Machine Image) — In-Depth

What is AMI?

A template for launching EC2s. Contains:

  • Root volume (OS + apps + config)
  • Launch permissions
  • Block device mapping

AMI Types

  1. AWS-provided — Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Windows Server
  2. AWS Marketplace — pre-built vendor AMIs (Bitnami, etc.)
  3. Community AMIs — shared by AWS users
  4. Custom AMI — yours, created from your EC2

AMI Lifecycle

  1. Configure EC2 (install apps, patches)
  2. Create AMI → automatically creates EBS snapshot
  3. Launch new EC2 from AMI → same state
  4. Distribute AMI across regions (copy)
  5. Share with other AWS accounts (permissions)

EC2 Image Builder

  • Automates AMI creation pipeline
  • Builds → tests → distributes → deprecates

  • Weekly patched golden AMIs
  • Compliance-hardened baselines
  • Standardized images across enterprise

🔥 SECTION 5: SECURITY — In-Depth

🛡️ Security Group (SG)

How it Works

  • Virtual firewall at instance/ENI level
  • Stateful — response traffic automatically allowed
  • Allow rules only (cannot deny)
  • Can reference other SGs, IPs, CIDRs, Prefix Lists
  • Multiple SGs per ENI (rules are additive)

✅ Use Cases:

  • Allow SSH (22) from office IP
  • Allow HTTPS (443) from internet
  • Allow DB (3306) from app tier SG only
  • Microservices communication

🛡️ NACL (Network Access Control List)

How it Works

  • Subnet-level firewall
  • Stateless — must explicitly allow in & out
  • Allow + Deny rules
  • Rules evaluated in numbered order (lowest first)
  • Default rule * denies if no match

✅ Use Cases:

  • Block malicious IPs at subnet level
  • Compliance rules requiring deny rules
  • Extra layer beyond SGs

🔐 IAM Roles for EC2 (Instance Profile)

How it Works

  1. Create IAM Role with policies (e.g., S3ReadOnly)
  2. Attach to EC2 via Instance Profile
  3. Apps on EC2 use SDK → credentials fetched from IMDS automatically
  4. Credentials auto-rotate

NEVER: Hardcode access keys on EC2.

✅ Use Cases:

  • EC2 reading from S3
  • EC2 writing logs to CloudWatch
  • EC2 calling DynamoDB
  • Auto Scaling EC2 accessing Secrets Manager

🔐 IMDS (Instance Metadata Service)

IMDSv1 vs IMDSv2

FeatureIMDSv1IMDSv2
Request typeGETPUT + Token
Session-based❌✅
SSRF protection❌✅

IMDSv2 prevents attackers from stealing credentials via SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery). Always enforce IMDSv2.

🔐 AWS Systems Manager Session Manager

How it Works

  • Browser-based or CLI shell to EC2
  • No port 22 open
  • No bastion host
  • No SSH keys
  • Logs every session to CloudWatch + S3
  • Works with private subnet EC2s (no public IP needed)

✅ Use Cases:

  • Secure admin access to production
  • Compliance auditing (all sessions logged)
  • Emergency access without VPN
  • Zero-trust architecture

🔥 SECTION 6: LOAD BALANCERS — In-Depth

⚖️ ALB (Application Load Balancer) — L7

Features

  • Path-based routing (/api/* vs /images/*)
  • Host-based routing (api.example.com vs web.example.com)
  • Header-based routing (route based on HTTP headers)
  • Query-string routing
  • WebSocket & HTTP/2
  • Redirect HTTP→HTTPS
  • Authentication (OIDC, Cognito)
  • Lambda target (invoke Lambda directly)

Target Types

  • Instance
  • IP (on-prem, VPC peering)
  • Lambda function
  • Another ALB

✅ Use Cases:

  • Microservices / containers (ECS, EKS)
  • Multi-tenant web apps
  • API routing (/v1/, /v2/)
  • Blue-green deployments

⚖️ NLB (Network Load Balancer) — L4

Features

  • Handles millions of req/sec
  • Ultra-low latency (~100 μs)
  • Static IP per AZ (can assign Elastic IPs)
  • TCP, UDP, TLS
  • Preserves source IP natively
  • TLS termination possible

✅ Use Cases:

  • Gaming servers (UDP)
  • IoT ingestion (MQTT over TCP)
  • Financial trading (ultra-low latency)
  • VoIP (RTP/RTCP)
  • Whitelisting required (static IP)

⚖️ GLB (Gateway Load Balancer) — L3/L4

Features

  • Routes traffic through 3rd-party network appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS)
  • GENEVE protocol (port 6081)
  • Transparent bump-in-the-wire inspection

✅ Use Cases:

  • Palo Alto, Fortinet, Check Point firewalls in AWS
  • Network security inspection
  • Centralized traffic inspection

⚖️ CLB (Classic Load Balancer) — Legacy

  • Deprecated, don't use in new designs.

🔥 SECTION 7: AUTO SCALING GROUP (ASG) — In-Depth

🚀 Core Components

  1. Launch Template (preferred) or Launch Configuration (legacy)
  2. Min / Desired / Max capacity
  3. Scaling policies
  4. Health checks
  5. Multi-AZ distribution

📈 Scaling Policies Deep Dive

1. Target Tracking (Recommended)

Maintain a metric at a target value.

  • Example: "Keep average CPU at 50%"
  • Auto-calculates scale-out/in actions

✅ Use Case: Simple, CPU/memory/request-count-based scaling

2. Step Scaling

Multiple thresholds with different actions.

  • CPU > 70% → add 2 instances
  • CPU > 90% → add 5 instances

✅ Use Case: Fine-grained control during varying load

3. Simple Scaling (Legacy)

Single threshold, cooldown between actions.

  • Avoid; use Step or Target Tracking.

4. Scheduled Scaling

Scale at specific times.

  • "Every weekday at 8 AM, scale to 10 instances"

✅ Use Case: Predictable traffic patterns (business hours)

5. Predictive Scaling

ML analyzes traffic patterns → pre-scales.

  • Handles recurring spikes (e.g., 9 AM rush) before they happen

✅ Use Case: Recurring, predictable load patterns

🚀 Key ASG Features

Lifecycle Hooks

Run custom actions before an instance:

  • Enters service (bootstrap, install agents, register with service discovery)
  • Exits service (deregister, drain, save logs)

✅ Use Case: Install config agents before traffic arrives

Warm Pool

Pre-initialized stopped instances ready to start rapidly.

  • Reduces scale-out time from minutes to seconds.

✅ Use Case: Fast response to unpredictable bursts

Cooldown Period

Prevents thrashing — waits before triggering another scaling action.

Health Checks

  • EC2 health (default) — based on EC2 status checks
  • ELB health — based on target health (recommended when behind ELB)

Mixed Instances Policy

Combine On-Demand + Spot across multiple instance types in one ASG.

✅ Use Case: Cost optimization with HA (save 70%+)

🔥 SECTION 8: PLACEMENT GROUPS — In-Depth

🌐 Cluster Placement Group

  • All instances in same rack, same AZ
  • Lowest network latency (< 1ms)
  • Highest packets-per-second
  • Single failure can take all out

✅ Use Cases:

  • HPC applications
  • Distributed ML training (with EFA)
  • Tightly-coupled simulations

🌐 Spread Placement Group

  • Each instance on distinct hardware

  • Financial ledger nodes

Private IP

  • Free

Public IP

  • Changes on stop/start
  • Free when instance running, costs nothing if not assigned

  • Survives instance stop
  • Charged when NOT associated with running instance
  • 5 per region (soft limit)

✅ Use Cases:

  • HA failover (move EIP to standby)

  • Saves in-memory state (RAM) to encrypted EBS root

🔥 SECTION 12: DISASTER RECOVERY — In-Depth

💥 DR Strategies

1. Backup & Restore (RTO: Hours)

  • Snapshots + AMIs copied to DR region
  • Restore when disaster strikes
  • Cheapest

✅ Use Cases: Non-critical apps, long RTO tolerance

2. Pilot Light (RTO: 10s of minutes)

  • Core minimal infra always running in DR region
  • DB replication active; web tier dormant
  • Scale up during DR

✅ Use Cases: Mid-criticality apps

3. Warm Standby (RTO: Minutes)

  • Full DR environment running, but scaled down
  • Scale up to match prod during DR

✅ Use Cases: Business-critical apps

4. Multi-Site Active/Active (RTO: Seconds)

  • Full prod in multiple regions
  • Route 53 traffic split / failover
  • Most expensive

✅ Use Cases: Mission-critical, zero-downtime apps (banking, e-commerce)

Network-attached block storage (like a virtual hard drive)
AZ-locked (exists in ONE AZ only)

EBS Volume Types — In Detail

Max IOPS: 16,000

Small-to-medium databases
Dev/test
🔸 gp2 (General Purpose SSD — Legacy)
Max IOPS: 16,000 (but scales at 3 IOPS per GB)

Incremental — only changed blocks are saved

Can be shared with other accounts
Can create AMI from snapshot

Creating test environments from prod snapshots

Linux-only

Root volume: DeleteOnTermination = true (default)
Additional volumes: DeleteOnTermination = false (default)

Allow rules only (cannot deny)
Can reference other SGs, IPs, CIDRs, Prefix Lists
Multiple SGs per ENI (rules are additive)

✅ Use Cases:

Allow SSH (22) from office IP
Allow HTTPS (443) from internet
Allow DB (3306) from app tier SG only
Microservices communication

How it Works
Subnet-level firewall
Stateless — must explicitly allow in & out
Allow + Deny rules
Rules evaluated in numbered order (lowest first)
Default rule * denies if no match

✅ Use Cases:

Block malicious IPs at subnet level
Compliance rules requiring deny rules
Extra layer beyond SGs
🔐 IAM Roles for EC2 (Instance Profile)
How it Works
Create IAM Role with policies (e.g., S3ReadOnly)
Attach to EC2 via Instance Profile
Apps on EC2 use SDK → credentials fetched from IMDS automatically
Credentials auto-rotate

EC2 reading from S3

EC2 calling DynamoDB
Auto Scaling EC2 accessing Secrets Manager

FEATURE	IMDSV1	IMDSV2

No bastion host
No SSH keys

Secure admin access to production

Emergency access without VPN
Zero-trust architecture

Handles millions of req/sec

TCP, UDP, TLS

VoIP (RTP/RTCP)
Whitelisting required (static IP)

Features

🎯 Load Balancer Decision Guide
REQUIREMENT	PICK
HTTP/HTTPS + smart routing	ALB

3rd-party firewall inspection	GLB
Lambda as target	ALB
Millions of connections/sec	NLB

🚀 Core Components

Scaling policies
Health checks

📈 Scaling Policies Deep Dive
1. Target Tracking (Recommended)

Maintain a metric at a target value.

Example: "Keep average CPU at 50%"
Auto-calculates scale-out/in actions

✅ Use Case: Simple, CPU/memory/request-count-based scaling

2. Step Scaling

Multiple thresholds with different actions.

CPU > 70% → add 2 instances
CPU > 90% → add 5 instances

✅ Use Case: Fine-grained control during varying load

3. Simple Scaling (Legacy)

Single threshold, cooldown between actions.

Avoid; use Step or Target Tracking.
4. Scheduled Scaling

Scale at specific times.

"Every weekday at 8 AM, scale to 10 instances"

✅ Use Case: Predictable traffic patterns (business hours)

5. Predictive Scaling

ML analyzes traffic patterns → pre-scales.

Handles recurring spikes (e.g., 9 AM rush) before they happen

🚀 Key ASG Features
Lifecycle Hooks

Run custom actions before an instance:

Enters service (bootstrap, install agents, register with service discovery)
Exits service (deregister, drain, save logs)

✅ Use Case: Install config agents before traffic arrives

Warm Pool

Reduces scale-out time from minutes to seconds.

✅ Use Case: Fast response to unpredictable bursts

Health Checks
EC2 health (default) — based on EC2 status checks
ELB health — based on target health (recommended when behind ELB)

✅ Use Case: Cost optimization with HA (save 70%+)

🔥 SECTION 8: PLACEMENT GROUPS — In-Depth

All instances in same rack, same AZ

✅ Use Cases:

HPC applications
Distributed ML training (with EFA)
Tightly-coupled simulations
🌐 Spread Placement Group
Each instance on distinct hardware
Max 7 instances per AZ
Max hardware isolation

✅ Use Cases:

Critical domain controllers (AD)
Master nodes of small HA clusters
Financial ledger nodes

Logical partitions (up to 7 per AZ)
Each partition on separate rack

✅ Use Cases:

HDFS / Hadoop
Cassandra
Kafka
Large distributed databases
🔥 SECTION 9: NETWORKING — In-Depth
🌐 IP Addressing
Private IP
Permanent within VPC
Free
Public IP
Changes on stop/start
Free when instance running, costs nothing if not assigned
Elastic IP (EIP)
Static public IPv4
Survives instance stop
Charged when NOT associated with running instance
5 per region (soft limit)

✅ Use Cases:

Fixed IP for whitelisting
HA failover (move EIP to standby)

🎯 Best Practice: Avoid EIP when possible → use ALB/NLB + Route 53 for scalable HA.

🌐 ENI / ENA / EFA (Summary)
COMPONENT	PURPOSE
ENI	Virtual NIC; IP/MAC failover, multi-homed EC2
ENA	Enhanced networking driver (100+ Gbps, Nitro default)

🌐 NAT Gateway
Managed NAT for private subnet outbound internet access
Per-AZ (deploy one per AZ for HA)
Up to 45 Gbps

🎯 Exam Trap: Single NAT GW = single-AZ failure = outage → always one NAT GW per AZ.

🔥 SECTION 10: INSTANCE LIFECYCLE — In-Depth
🔁 Lifecycle States
ACTION	EBS	RAM	INSTANCE STORE	BILLING
Reboot	Kept	Kept	Kept	Continues
Stop	Kept	Lost	LOST	EBS only
Hibernate	Kept	Saved to EBS root	LOST	EBS + EIP

*If DeleteOnTermination = true

🌙 Hibernation Deep Dive
Saves in-memory state (RAM) to encrypted EBS root
Resume in seconds → memory, processes, connections restored
Requirements:
Nitro-based instance
EBS-backed root, encrypted
RAM ≤ 150 GB
Supported OS (Amazon Linux 2, Ubuntu, Windows)

✅ Use Cases:

Apps with long warm-up (ML models, JVMs, caches)
Dev environments paused overnight
Batch jobs resumed after interruption
🔥 SECTION 11: MONITORING — In-Depth
📊 CloudWatch Default Metrics (Free)

✅ CPU Utilization ✅ Network In/Out ✅ Disk Read/Write (I/O count, bytes) ✅ Status Checks (system + instance)

❌ NOT Default (Requires CloudWatch Agent)
Memory (RAM) usage
Disk space used (not I/O — space on filesystem)
Process-level metrics
Custom application metrics
🔍 Status Checks
System Status Check
Monitors AWS infrastructure (host, network, power)
Failure = AWS issue → Solution: Stop/Start instance (moves to new host)
Instance Status Check
Monitors your OS/software (kernel, network config)
Failure = your issue → Fix OS/config
🔄 EC2 Auto-Recovery
CloudWatch alarm triggers automatic recovery on system check failure
Same instance ID, IP, metadata → no reconfiguration needed

✅ Use Case: Stateful EC2 that must recover automatically on host failure

🔥 SECTION 12: DISASTER RECOVERY — In-Depth
💥 DR Strategies
1. Backup & Restore (RTO: Hours)
Snapshots + AMIs copied to DR region
Restore when disaster strikes
Cheapest

✅ Use Cases: Non-critical apps, long RTO tolerance

2. Pilot Light (RTO: 10s of minutes)
Core minimal infra always running in DR region
DB replication active; web tier dormant
Scale up during DR

✅ Use Cases: Mid-criticality apps

3. Warm Standby (RTO: Minutes)
Full DR environment running, but scaled down
Scale up to match prod during DR

✅ Use Cases: Business-critical apps

4. Multi-Site Active/Active (RTO: Seconds)
Full prod in multiple regions
Route 53 traffic split / failover
Most expensive

✅ Use Cases: Mission-critical, zero-downtime apps (banking, e-commerce)

🎯 DR Decision Guide
NEED	STRATEGY
Cheapest, long RTO OK	Backup & Restore
Balanced cost/RTO	Pilot Light
Low RTO	Warm Standby
Near-zero downtime	Multi-Site Active/Active
⚡ TOP 30 EXAM TRAPS — MEMORIZE!
EBS is AZ-locked → use snapshot to move
Multi-Attach only on io1/io2
Instance Store LOST on stop
Snapshots stored in S3 (managed)
AMIs are region-specific → copy to new region
Spot = 90% off but interruptible (2-min warning)
Dedicated Host = BYOL / socket visibility
Dedicated Instance = hardware isolation only
Convertible RI if you need family flexibility
Compute Savings Plan covers EC2 + Fargate + Lambda
NLB = static IP, ALB = dynamic
NLB preserves source IP; ALB uses X-Forwarded-For
UDP → only NLB
Lambda target → only ALB
SG = stateful, allow only
NACL = stateless, allow + deny
Memory metric needs CloudWatch Agent
IMDSv2 > IMDSv1
Session Manager > Bastion Host
Hibernation requires encrypted EBS root, RAM < 150 GB
Public IP changes on stop/start → use EIP
Unused Elastic IP = charged
NAT Gateway per AZ for HA
ASG is free, pay only EC2
Launch Template > Launch Configuration
Target Tracking = easiest ASG policy
Warm Pool speeds up scale-out
Cluster PG = low latency, Spread = isolation, Partition = big data
EFS = multi-AZ shared Linux file system
FSx for Windows = SMB + AD; FSx for Lustre = HPC/ML
🎯 QUICK-PICK CHEAT SHEET
KEYWORD	PICK
Fault-tolerant batch	Spot
24/7 production	Reserved Instance
BYOL Oracle/Windows	Dedicated Host
Shared multi-AZ file system	EFS
Windows file share	FSx for Windows
HPC file system	FSx for Lustre
Highest EBS IOPS	io2 Block Express
Cheapest EBS HDD	sc1
Static public IP	Elastic IP / NLB
Path-based routing	ALB
UDP / static IP LB	NLB
No port 22, audit	Session Manager
Block specific IP	NACL
HPC low latency	Cluster PG + EFA
Kafka/Cassandra	Partition PG
Monitor RAM	CloudWatch Agent
Preserve RAM state	Hibernate
Move EBS across AZs	Snapshot → Restore
Scale at 9 AM daily	Scheduled Scaling
Pre-warm EC2	Warm Pool
📝 10 MCQs WITH EXPLANATIONS

Q1: Fault-tolerant nightly batch job, cheapest? → Spot Instances ✅ (up to 90% off, interruption tolerated)

Q2: Per-socket license compliance for Oracle? → Dedicated Host ✅ (only option with socket visibility)

Q3: Shared storage across EC2 fleet in 3 AZs? → EFS ✅ (EBS is AZ-locked)

Q4: Customer firewall needs to whitelist LB IP? → NLB ✅ (static IP per AZ; ALB IPs change)

Q5: Secure access to private EC2 with audit logs, no port 22? → SSM Session Manager ✅ (logs to CloudWatch/S3, no SSH)

Q6: Cassandra cluster with rack-level isolation? → Partition Placement Group ✅ (partitions on separate racks)

Q7: Move EBS to another AZ? → Snapshot → Restore in new AZ ✅ (EBS is AZ-locked)

Q8: Monitor RAM on EC2? → Install CloudWatch Agent ✅ (RAM isn't default)

Q9: Same public IP after reboot? → Elastic IP ✅ (public IP changes on stop/start)

Q10: DB needs 200,000 IOPS? → io2 Block Express ✅ (up to 256,000 IOPS)

title: EC2 Fundamentals
body:
📘 Category 1: EC2 Instance Types — Deep Dive

Instance Family Decision Matrix (🔥 Must Memorize)

FamilyPrefixOptimized ForSAA Scenario
General PurposeT (burstable), M, A (ARM/Graviton), MacBalancedWeb apps, microservices, small-mid DBs
Compute OptimizedCCPU-intensiveGaming servers, HPC, batch, ML inference, video encoding
Memory OptimizedR, X, z1d, High Memory (u-)RAM-heavySAP HANA, Redis, Elasticsearch, real-time big data
Storage OptimizedI (NVMe SSD), D (HDD), H, Im4gn, Is4genHigh IOPS / throughputNoSQL (Cassandra), data warehouse, Hadoop, HDFS
Accelerated ComputingP (GPU ML training), G (GPU graphics), Inf (inference), Trn (training), F (FPGA)GPU/FPGAML training (P4), video rendering (G5), inference (Inf2)

Burstable vs Fixed Performance (🔥 SAA Trap)

  • T-family (T3, T3a, T4g): Baseline CPU + CPU credits. Burst above baseline consumes credits.
  • T3 Unlimited mode: Can burst indefinitely, pay extra if credits exhausted.
  • T3 Standard mode: Throttled to baseline when credits run out.

🎯 Scenario: A dev/test web server with unpredictable low traffic → T3 Standard (cheapest). A small production API with occasional spikes where performance matters more than cost → T3 Unlimited.

Graviton (ARM) Instances

  • Up to 40% better price/performance than x86
  • Instance suffix: g (e.g., m6g, c7g, r7g)
  • 🎯 Scenario: Cost-optimization question where the app is compiled for ARM (or runs on Linux/container) → Graviton.

📘 Category 2: Pricing Models — SAA Decision Logic

ModelDiscountCommitmentInterruptionExam Keyword
On-Demand0%NoneNo"Short-term, unpredictable"
Reserved Instance (Standard)~72%1 or 3 yrNo"Steady-state, known workload"
Reserved Instance (Convertible)~54%1 or 3 yrNo"Need to change family later"
Compute Savings Plan~66%1 or 3 yr ($/hr commit)No"Flexibility across EC2/Fargate/Lambda, any region/family"
EC2 Instance Savings Plan~72%1 or 3 yrNo"Specific family in region, want AZ/size flexibility"
Spot Instances~90%NoneYes (2-min warning)"Fault-tolerant, stateless, flexible start/end"
Spot Fleet / EC2 FleetMixedNoneMixed"Blend Spot + On-Demand at scale"
Dedicated HostHighest costOptionalNo"BYOL, compliance, socket/core visibility"
Dedicated InstanceModerateNoneNo"Hardware isolation, no socket visibility"
Capacity ReservationsNo discountNoneNo"Guarantee capacity in specific AZ for event"

🔥 SAA Decision Tree for Pricing

  1. Can it be interrupted? → Yes → Spot
  2. Long-term, predictable? → RI or Savings Plan
  3. Need hardware isolation + license compliance? → Dedicated Host
  4. Need guaranteed capacity for known spike? → On-Demand Capacity Reservations
  5. Mix of steady + spiky? → RI for baseline + Spot/On-Demand for spikes

🎯 Real scenario: Media company transcodes videos — each job is idempotent and retryable → Spot Fleet saves 70–90% vs On-Demand.

🎯 Real scenario: Oracle DB with BYOL requiring per-socket licensing audit → Dedicated Host (only option that exposes socket/core).

📘 Category 3: Storage — EBS, Instance Store, EFS, FSx

3.1 EBS Volume Types (🔥 Super High Exam Weight)

TypeMax IOPSMax ThroughputMax SizeUse Case
gp3 (SSD)16,0001,000 MB/s16 TiBDefault; IOPS/throughput decoupled from size. Cost-effective.
gp2 (SSD)16,000250 MB/s16 TiBOlder gen; IOPS scales with size (3 IOPS/GB)
io2 Block Express (SSD)256,0004,000 MB/s64 TiBHighest performance; SAP HANA, critical DBs
io1 / io2 (SSD)64,0001,000 MB/s16 TiBHigh-performance DBs; supports Multi-Attach
st1 (HDD)500500 MB/s16 TiBBig data, log processing, data warehouse (sequential)
sc1 (HDD)250250 MB/s16 TiBCold, infrequently accessed; cheapest

🔥 Key EBS Concepts for SAA

  • AZ-locked: EBS lives in ONE AZ. To move to another AZ → snapshot → restore in new AZ.
  • Snapshots are incremental, stored in S3 (managed by AWS, not in your bucket).
  • EBS Multi-Attach: Only io1/io2 can attach to up to 16 Nitro instances in same AZ → used for clustered apps (but app must handle concurrent writes, e.g., with cluster-aware FS).
  • Encryption: Uses KMS. To encrypt an unencrypted volume → snapshot → copy snapshot with encryption → create volume.
  • Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR): Eliminates the lazy-load penalty when restoring large volumes → critical for DR with low RTO.
  • EBS-Optimized instances: Dedicated bandwidth between EC2 and EBS.

🎯 Scenario: A MySQL DB needs 20,000 IOPS sustained → io2 (gp3 maxes at 16k). 🎯 Scenario: Restore 2 TB volume from snapshot, need immediate full performance → enable FSR. 🎯 Scenario: Shared file system across 2+ EC2 for a cluster → NOT EBS (except io2 Multi-Attach) → usually EFS.

3.2 Instance Store

  • Ephemeral NVMe SSD physically attached to host.
  • Highest IOPS/throughput available.
  • Lost on stop, hibernate, or hardware failure.
  • 🎯 Scenario: Buffer/cache for a high-performance app (e.g., Cassandra, Kafka replicas) → Instance Store (data replicated at app layer).

3.3 EFS vs FSx vs EBS (🔥 Common Exam Trap)

EBSEFSFSx for WindowsFSx for Lustre
TypeBlockFile (NFS)File (SMB)High-perf file
OSLinux/WindowsLinux onlyWindowsLinux
Multi-AZNo (AZ-locked)Yes (Regional)OptionalSingle-AZ (or Multi)
Concurrent mountsLimited (Multi-Attach)1000s of EC2ManyMany
Use caseSingle-instance diskShared Linux workloads, CMSWindows file shares, AD-integratedHPC, ML, media

🎯 Scenario: WordPress fleet across 3 AZs needing shared media files → EFS. 🎯 Scenario: Windows .NET app needing SMB share joined to AD → FSx for Windows. 🎯 Scenario: Training ML models on S3 data with ultra-low latency → FSx for Lustre.

📘 Category 4: AMI, Snapshots & Golden Images

  • AMI = EBS Snapshot + metadata + launch permissions
  • AMIs are region-scoped → copy to other regions for DR / global launches.
  • EBS-backed AMI: Root is EBS → can stop instance.
  • Instance-store-backed AMI: Root is ephemeral → cannot stop, only terminate.

EC2 Image Builder

  • Automates AMI creation, patching, testing, distribution across regions/accounts.
  • 🎯 Scenario: Enterprise wants weekly patched golden AMIs distributed to 10 accounts → EC2 Image Builder + RAM.

📘 Category 5: Networking Deep Dive

5.1 ENI, ENA, EFA

InterfacePurpose
ENI (Elastic Network Interface)Virtual NIC; can attach/detach for failover, multi-homing
ENA (Elastic Network Adapter)Enhanced networking up to 100 Gbps
EFA (Elastic Fabric Adapter)HPC/ML — OS bypass, used for MPI workloads

🎯 Scenario: Tightly-coupled HPC cluster running MPI → EFA + Cluster Placement Group.

5.2 Placement Groups (🔥 SAA Favorite)

TypePlacementUse Case
ClusterSame rack, same AZLowest latency, HPC, distributed ML
SpreadDistinct hardwareSmall number of critical instances (max 7/AZ)
PartitionLogical partitions, each on separate rackBig data (HDFS, Kafka, Cassandra) — up to 7 partitions per AZ

🎯 Scenario: Cassandra cluster with 20 nodes needing rack awareness → Partition Placement Group. 🎯 Scenario: 5 critical domain controllers must never fail together → Spread Placement Group.

5.3 IP Addressing

  • Private IP: Stays with instance until terminated.
  • Public IP: Changes on stop/start.
  • Elastic IP (EIP): Static public IPv4. Free when attached to running instance; charged when unused. Limit 5/region (soft).

🎯 SAA tip: Whenever possible, avoid EIP → use ALB/NLB + DNS (Route 53) for failover, which is more scalable.

📘 Category 6: High Availability, Scaling & Load Balancing

6.1 Elastic Load Balancer (🔥 Top SAA Topic)

LBLayerProtocolsKey FeaturesScenario
ALBL7HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, gRPCPath-based, host-based, header-based routing; integrates with WAF, Cognito, Lambda targetMicroservices, containers (ECS/EKS), multi-tenant apps
NLBL4TCP, UDP, TLSMillions req/sec, ultra-low latency, static IP per AZ, preserves source IPGaming (UDP), IoT, financial trading, needing static IPs
GLB (Gateway LB)L3/4 (GENEVE)IPDeploys 3rd-party appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS) inlineTransparent traffic inspection via Palo Alto, Fortinet
CLB (Classic)L4/L7HTTP, HTTPS, TCPLegacy — avoid in new designsOnly for EC2-Classic

ALB Advanced Features (SAA hotspot)

  • Target types: Instance, IP, Lambda, ALB (ALB-to-ALB)
  • Sticky sessions (session affinity) via cookies
  • SNI: Multiple SSL certs on one ALB
  • Redirect HTTP→HTTPS, fixed response, authentication (OIDC/Cognito)

🎯 Scenario: Route /api/* to one target group, /images/* to another → ALB path-based routing. 🎯 Scenario: Need static IP whitelisted by customer firewall → NLB (ALB has dynamic IPs).

6.2 Auto Scaling Group (ASG) (🔥 Exam-Critical)

Core components:

  • Launch Template (preferred over Launch Configuration — supports versioning, mixed instances, Spot)
  • Min / Desired / Max capacity
  • Scaling policies

Scaling Policy Types:

TypeHow It WorksExample
Target TrackingMaintain metric at target (e.g., CPU 50%)Easiest, recommended
Step ScalingAdd N instances when CPU > X for Y minFine-grained control
Simple ScalingLegacy, one adjustment then cooldownAvoid in new designs
Scheduled ScalingScale at known time (e.g., 9 AM weekdays)Predictable traffic
Predictive ScalingML-based, forecasts and pre-scalesRecurring patterns

ASG + ELB integration:

  • ASG registers new instances with target group automatically.
  • ELB health checks can replace unhealthy instances.
  • Cooldown period prevents thrashing.
  • Warm Pool: Pre-initialized stopped instances → faster scale-out.
  • Lifecycle hooks: Run script before/after instance joins or leaves ASG.

🎯 Scenario: E-commerce during Black Friday → Predictive + Scheduled Scaling. 🎯 Scenario: Need instance to bootstrap & register with config server before serving traffic → Lifecycle hook (pending:wait).

6.3 Designing for HA

  • Multi-AZ: ASG + ELB spanning ≥ 2 AZs = baseline HA.
  • Multi-Region: Route 53 failover/latency routing + cross-region replication.
  • RTO/RPO decisions drive DR strategy:
    • Backup & Restore (hours) – snapshots to another region.
    • Pilot Light – minimal always-on in DR region.
    • Warm Standby – scaled-down active version.
    • Multi-Site Active/Active – full prod in multiple regions.

📘 Category 7: Security — SAA Focus

7.1 Security Groups vs NACLs (🔥 Recurring Trap)

FeatureSecurity GroupNACL
ScopeInstance (ENI)Subnet
StateStatefulStateless
RulesAllow onlyAllow + Deny
EvaluationAll rules evaluatedRules numbered, first match wins
ReferenceOther SGs, IPsIPs/CIDR only

🎯 Scenario: Block a specific malicious IP → NACL deny rule (SG can't deny). 🎯 Scenario: Allow web tier to talk to app tier without hardcoding IPs → SG referencing SG.

7.2 IAM Roles for EC2 (Instance Profile)

  • Credentials delivered via IMDS (Instance Metadata Service).
  • IMDSv2 (session-based, token-required) — recommended, defeats SSRF attacks.
  • Never embed access keys on instances.

🎯 Scenario: EC2 app needs S3 + DynamoDB → IAM Role attached to instance, app uses SDK default credentials chain.

7.3 EC2 Instance Connect & Session Manager

  • Systems Manager Session Manager: Shell access without SSH, without bastion, without open port 22. Logs sessions to CloudWatch/S3.
  • EC2 Instance Connect: Push temporary SSH key via API.

🎯 Scenario: Audit requires no open inbound SSH and session logging → SSM Session Manager.

7.4 Encryption

  • EBS: AES-256 via KMS (data, snapshots, AMIs).
  • In-transit: TLS via ALB/NLB listeners.
  • Enforce default EBS encryption at account level.

📘 Category 8: Hibernation, Stop, Reboot, Terminate

ActionEBS dataRAMBillingPublic IP
RebootKeptKeptContinuesSame
StopKeptLostEBS onlyLost (new on start)
HibernateKeptSaved to EBS rootEBS + EIPLost
TerminateDeleted (if DeleteOnTermination)LostStopsReleased

Hibernation requirements: EBS root, encrypted, RAM < 150 GB, supported instance families.

🎯 Scenario: Long-running in-memory cache that takes 20 min to warm up; want to pause overnight to save money → Hibernate.

📘 Category 9: Monitoring & Troubleshooting

  • CloudWatch default metrics (1 or 5 min): CPU, Network, Disk I/O (not disk usage), Status Checks.
  • NOT default: Memory, Disk space usage, Process-level → need CloudWatch Agent.
  • Status Checks:
    • System status check fails → AWS infrastructure issue → stop/start instance to move hosts.
    • Instance status check fails → OS/config issue → you must fix.
  • EventBridge can auto-recover failed instances.

🎯 Scenario: RAM-sensitive app needs alerts on >80% memory → Install CloudWatch Agent + custom metric + alarm.

📘 Category 10: Common SAA Scenario Patterns

Pattern 1: Cost-Optimized Stateless Web App

  • ALB + ASG (Mixed Instances Policy) with On-Demand base + Spot → save up to 70%.

Pattern 2: Secure 3-Tier Architecture

  • Web tier in public subnet behind ALB
  • App tier in private subnet, SG allows only from Web SG

TYPE	MAX IOPS	MAX THROUGHPUT	MAX SIZE	USE CASE

gp2 (SSD)	16,000	250 MB/s	16 TiB	Older gen; IOPS scales with size (3 IOPS/GB)

🔥 Key EBS Concepts for SAA
AZ-locked: EBS lives in ONE AZ. To move to another AZ → snapshot → restore in new AZ.
Snapshots are incremental, stored in S3 (managed by AWS, not in your bucket).
EBS Multi-Attach: Only io1/io2 can attach to up to 16 Nitro instances in same AZ → used for clustered apps (but app must handle concurrent writes, e.g., with cluster-aware FS).
Encryption: Uses KMS. To encrypt an unencrypted volume → snapshot → copy snapshot with encryption → create volume.
Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR): Eliminates the lazy-load penalty when restoring large volumes → critical for DR with low RTO.
EBS-Optimized instances: Dedicated bandwidth between EC2 and EBS.

Lost on stop, hibernate, or hardware failure.
🎯 Scenario: Buffer/cache for a high-performance app (e.g., Cassandra, Kafka replicas) → Instance Store (data replicated at app layer).

Type	Block	File (NFS)	File (SMB)	High-perf file
OS	Linux/Windows	Linux only	Windows	Linux
